name: Cellulitis

likely: Staphylococcus aureus (more likely if purulent drainage or abscess present)
possible: MRSA (if risk factors: prior MRSA, IV drug use, recent hospitalization)
pathogens.why: Non-purulent cellulitis is predominantly streptococcal. Purulent cellulitis or associated abscess shifts likelihood toward S. aureus, including MRSA in at-risk populations, changing the empiric choice accordingly.

investigations.test: None routinely required for typical mild-moderate cellulitis
investigations.why: Diagnosis is clinical; cultures of intact cellulitic skin have low yield.

investigations.test: Blood cultures (if systemically unwell or immunocompromised)
investigations.why: Identifies bacteremic spread in more severe presentations.
Identifies organism and susceptibility, particularly important given variable MRSA prevalence.
Supports severity assessment and provides a baseline to track response.

references: IDSA Skin and Soft Tissue Infection Guidelines
reason: Crepitus or bullae formation raises concern for necrotizing soft tissue infection - this requires urgent surgical evaluation in addition to antibiotics, not antibiotics alone.
Empiric antibiotics targeting streptococci (and staphylococci if purulent) are indicated.

clinicalPearls: Non-purulent cellulitis (no associated abscess, focal purulence, or drainage) is a rapidly spreading, diffuse process typically due to S. pyogenes, often accompanied by lymphangitis and fever; purulent cellulitis arising from a focal lesion (furuncle, carbuncle, abscess, surgical wound) is more likely staphylococcal (Harrison 22e p.1095).

Even with needle aspiration of the advancing edge or punch biopsy of involved tissue, cultures are positive in only about 20% of cases, suggesting low bacterial numbers and that much of the spreading erythema is driven by extracellular toxins and host inflammatory mediators (Harrison 22e p.1095).

When a draining wound or visible portal of entry is present, Gram stain and culture of that material can give a definitive microbiologic diagnosis, unlike cultures of intact cellulitic skin (Harrison 22e p.1095).

A careful exposure/epidemiologic history is diagnostically valuable because many less common causative organisms occupy characteristic ecological niches (e.g., cat/dog bite, freshwater laceration, fish/swine handling, aquarium water) (Harrison 22e p.1095).
Bilateral, symmetric lower-leg involvement favors a mimic such as stasis dermatitis, whereas true cellulitis is usually unilateral (Harrison 22e p.428).
harrison.pathophysiology: Bacteria reach the dermis and subcutaneous soft tissue after disruption of the epidermal barrier by cracks, abrasions, cuts, burns, insect bites, surgical incisions, IV catheters, trauma, tinea/fungal infection, or pressure and venous-stasis ulcers. Organisms already colonizing the skin (notably S. aureus and group A streptococci) most readily exploit such breaks, though many exogenous bacteria can be introduced. Streptococcal disease characteristically spreads diffusely via lymphatics, producing lymphangitis, whereas staphylococcal disease spreads from a central focus such as an abscess or infected foreign body. Much of the expanding erythema reflects the action of bacterial extracellular toxins and host-derived inflammatory mediators rather than high bacterial burden. Progression to deeper structures with loss of vascular integrity (purple bullae, ecchymosis, cutaneous anesthesia) signals possible necrotizing infection (Harrison 22e p.1095, p.1007).
additionalDifferentials: Erysipelas (S. pyogenes superficial dermal/lymphatic infection with sharply demarcated, raised, indurated borders and abrupt fiery-red swelling) (Harrison 22e p.1095)
Necrotizing fasciitis / deeper necrotizing soft-tissue infection (Harrison 22e p.1095)
Purulent cellulitis associated with a focal staphylococcal lesion such as a furuncle, carbuncle, or abscess (Harrison 22e p.1095)
infectionMimics: Herpes zoster (dermatomal vesicular eruption may be mistaken for cellulitis early) (Harrison 22e p.93)
nonInfectiousMimics: Stasis dermatitis, which when acutely inflamed with crusting and exudate is easily confused with cellulitis; symmetric bilateral leg involvement favors stasis dermatitis (Harrison 22e p.428, p.436)
additionalInvestigations: Gram stain and culture of drainage, open wound, or identifiable portal of entry when present, for definitive etiology (Harrison 22e p.1095)
Needle aspiration of the leading edge or punch biopsy of involved skin in selected cases, recognizing low (~20%) culture yield (Harrison 22e p.1095)
redFlags: Purple/hemorrhagic bullae, ecchymosis, or cutaneous anesthesia suggesting loss of vascular integrity and possible necrotizing fasciitis or myonecrosis (Harrison 22e p.1095)
Pain or tenderness disproportionate to visible skin findings, or unexplained fever with deep soft-tissue pain even without overt skin inflammation (Harrison 22e p.1095)
Brawny edema, dark-red induration, skin friability with bluish/maroon/black discoloration, or systemic toxicity/shock indicating deep necrotizing infection (Harrison 22e p.1095)
pitfalls: Routine cultures of intact cellulitic skin are frequently negative (positive in only ~20% even with aspiration or biopsy), so negative cultures do NOT exclude cellulitis (Harrison 22e p.1095).

When patients labeled 'cellulitis' are reviewed by dermatology, roughly one-third have an alternative diagnosis (e.g., eczema, lymphedema), so an overcall risks unnecessary hospitalization and antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.93).
Bilateral symmetric lower-extremity erythema is more likely stasis dermatitis than cellulitis (Harrison 22e p.428).
Early necrotizing fasciitis may present with pain or unexplained fever as the only manifestation; do NOT rely on overt cutaneous inflammation to exclude it (Harrison 22e p.1095).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison distinguishes non-purulent cellulitis (diffuse, spreading, typically streptococcal, often with lymphangitis and fever) from purulent cellulitis (associated with a focal lesion such as furuncle, carbuncle, abscess, or surgical wound, typically staphylococcal, the FDA-preferred term for these). Loss of vascular integrity (purple bullae, ecchymosis, cutaneous anesthesia, systemic toxicity) marks progression toward necrotizing infection (Harrison 22e p.1095).
